definition: Noun Censored spelling of shittery .
Noun ( Islam ) Religious views. Borrowed from Arabic عَقِيدَة (ʕaqīda).
Noun (Australia, slang) A barracouta.
Verb Pronunciation spelling of hear . A representation of the pronunciation of hear by a speaker whose dialect lacks the voiceless glottal fricative or transition ([h]).

/əm/ Pronoun ( now colloquial ) Them (now only in unstressed position). From earlier hem , from Middle English hem , from Old English heom (“them”, dative) of hie , originally a dative plural form but in Middle English coming to serve as an accusative plural as well. Cognate with Dutch hun (“them”), German ihnen (“them”). Now often treated as a colloquial apheretic form of them , which however derives from Old Norse rather than Old English.
Adverb ( dialectal ) Pronunciation spelling of how .
Noun ( colloquial ) Clipping of potato .

Suffix (Internet slang, leetspeak, nonstandard) General-purpose suffix for purposes of "leet" respelling, sometimes replacing -er or -or . Perhaps derived from -er , with influence from the Latinate -or . Spelling due to leet.

/æk/ Suffix One affected with. Of, belonging to. Used to form the names of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) that are derivatives of acetic acid. From French -acque , from New Latin -acus , from Ancient Greek -ακός (-akós, “-ic”). Related to -ic and -y . From acetic acid, which is used in the synthesis of many of these compounds.
/ˈam.ɪ.vɪə/, /ˈæm.ɪˌvɪɹ/ Suffix ( pharmacology ) Used to form names of neuraminidase inhibitors used as antivirals. From (neur)ami(nidase) +‎ -vir (“antiviral”).
/æstɪk/ Suffix Used to form adjectives from nouns, often with the meaning meaning "of, or relating to". Equivalent to -ast +‎ -ic
/ˈeɪ.zə(ʊ).læm/, /ˈæz.əˌlæm/ Suffix ( pharmacology ) Used to form names of diazepam derivatives. Blend of azole +‎ -azepam .
/ˈeɪ.zəs.ɪn/ Suffix ( pharmacology ) Used to form names of prazosin derivatives used as antihypertensive substances. From prazosin .
Suffix carried or spread by From borne , past participle of bear .
Suffix Forming nouns relating to a bending or curvature. From Ancient Greek κάμψις (kámpsis).
Suffix (after 1 , 2 , or 3 ) Times: used to form a multiplicative numeral from a cardinal numeral.

/tʃ(j)æ/, /tʃ(j)ə/ Usage Note Sometimes written as a separate word ( cha ). From an unstressed you (/jə/) after a word ending in /t/; the unstressed sequence /tj/ coalesces into /tʃ/ ⟨ch⟩ in many accents. Compare di dja .
/klɪ.diːn/ Suffix ( pharmacology ) Used to form names of muscarinic receptor agonists and antagonists. From quinuclidine or (cy)cl(o)- +‎ -idine .

/-kɹæt/ Suffix A participant in a specified form of government. An advocate of a specified form of government. From Ancient Greek κράτος (krátos, “power, might”), modelled after words of Ancient Greek origin such as democrat and aristocrat . From Proto-Indo-European *kret- (English hard ).
/kjəˈɹoʊ.ni.əm/, /kjʊˈɹəʊ.ni.əm/ Suffix ( pharmacology ) Used to form names of neuromuscular blocking agents with rigid structure. From cur(are) +‎ -onium (“quaternary ammonium compound”).
/-ˈdiːsɪs/, /-ˌdɪs.ɪs/ Suffix ( medicine ) Binding, fusion. Borrowed from Ancient Greek δέσῐς (désĭs, “binding together”), from δέω (déō, “to bind, tie, fasten”) +‎ -σῐς (-sĭs, nominal suffix).

/-in/, /-iːn/ Suffix Forms adjectives relating to places and nouns for their inhabitants. Forms adjectives and nouns denoting religious groups from personal names. ( organic chemistry ) An unsaturated hydrocarbon having at least one double bond; an alkene. ( organic chemistry ) An aromatic hydrocarbon based on benzene. A polymer derived from an alkene. A single-atom thick two-dimensional layer of atoms. Borrowed from Latin -ēnus , from Ancient Greek -ηνός (-ēnós), forming adjectives from place n...
Suffix Forming nouns denoting female people, usually from terms ending in French -eur . Borrowed from French -euse .

Suffix The act of creating something, or ( more broadly ) any process involving the specified thing. Borrowed from French -faction , from Latin -factiō . This is the ending that arises when forming action nouns using -tiō (equivalent to English -tion ) from compound verbs ending in -faciō (“to make, to do”), which carry a causative meaning. For example, liqueō (“to be liquid”) +‎ faciō > liquefaciō (“to make (something) liquid”) > liquefactiō > English liquefaction . The suffix was later app...

Suffix Used to form nouns denoting the process of producing or making something. Clipping of manufacture , ultimately from Latin factus (“done, made”), perfect passive participle of faciō (“to do, make”).
Infix ( vulgar ) Pronunciation spelling of -fucking- .

Infix ( vulgar ) An intensifier. Synonyms: -bloody-, -goddamn-, -motherfucking- Usage Note It is generally inserted before the stressed syllable, but may also be inserted between the prefix and the base. Words containing this infix may be spelled with or without hyphens, up to authorial preference. When placed between words in a phrase or name, this infix is usually written with spaces. Euphemisms such as -flipping- and -freaking- tend to be used when intentionally avoiding vulgar words. Tmetic ...

/-ˈɪʃən/ Suffix forming nouns denoting occupations: A person who studies or is an expert in the related -ics. Usage Note Relatively few terms are directly derived using this suffix. Terms ending in -ician were often derived from Middle French words ending in -icien , which themselves were derived from words ending in -ique f sg + -ien , e.g.: From French -icien , from -ique f sg +‎ -ien . By surface analysis, -ic +‎ -ian .

/ɪfaɪ/ Suffix Forms transitive verbs meaning "to make" from adjectives and nouns. Forms intransitive verbs meaning "to become" from adjectives and nouns. From Middle English -ifien , from Old French -ifier , from Latin -ificāre , from -ficus , from faciō (“to make, do”). For example, purify from purificare , from purificus .
/ɪm.əs/ Suffix ( pharmacology ) Used to form names of immunosuppressants other than antineoplastics. Contraction of immunosuppressant .

Suffix Used to form feminine nouns. Synonym: -ine Used to form names of musical instruments. From Italian -ina and its etymon Classical Latin -īna . In some instances perhaps also partly via Spanish -ina . Doublet of -ine .

Suffix A component of some female given names. Latinized form of Germanic name suffix -lind , -linde (“tender, soft”), such as Sieglinde and Dietlinde , from Proto-Germanic *linþiz (“gentle, mild”) (English lithe ). Found in names such as Old High German Irmilinda and Old Dutch Frithelind . See lind , Linda .

Suffix Used to form adverbs describing action in the manner of the root adjective; use is identical irrespective of whether the root adjective ends with -istic or -istical . Alternately -istical (“adjective suffix”) + -ly (“adverb suffix”) or -istic (“adjective suffix”) + -ally (“adverb suffix”). In either case, ultimately -ist + -ic + -al + -ly .
Infix (slang, African-American Vernacular) An intensifier. From a style of cant used by African Americans in the 1970s and popularized by rapper Snoop Dogg. See -izzle for more.
Suffix Forms names of speech disorders. Features in Latin names of rhetoric figures. From Ancient Greek -λογία (-logía, “speech”).

Suffix to carry out a specified form of divination (fandom slang, video games) A suffix attached to a noun or character's name to create a word for an in-game romance subplot or mechanic. From a rebracketing of romance .
Suffix (paper, printing) Used to form page and book sizes. From Latin ending and apparent suffix of cardinal numbers.
/məbiːl/ Suffix Used to form nouns meaning a particular type of vehicle, particularly one to transport the person or thing described by the word to which the suffix is attached.
/moʊˈɹɛl.ɪn/, /məʊˈɹɛl.ɪn/ Suffix ( pharmacology ) Used to form names of growth hormone release–stimulating peptides. From [Term?] +‎ -relin (“pituitary hormone release–stimulating peptide”).

/ˈmaɪ.sɪn/ Suffix ( pharmacology ) Used to form names of antibiotics produced by Streptomyces strains. ( pharmacology ) Used to form names of antibiotics that pertain to fungi From streptomycin . From Ancient Greek μύκης (múkēs, “fungus”).
/nək.lɪn/ Suffix ( pharmacology ) Nicotinic cholinergic receptor partial agonist/agonist. Probably blend of nicotine +‎ choline .
Suffix Appended to titles of (often fictional) machines, especially to suggest that the verb to which the suffix is appended is its primary function. Back-formation from automatic .
Suffix Used to convert the name of an atom or ion to an adjective that means containing cations or anions of that atom or ion. Suffixal construction from -o(us) +‎ -an .
Suffix ( medicine ) pain From international scientific vocabulary, reflecting a New Latin combining form, from Ancient Greek ὀδύνη (odúnē, “sorrow, grief, anguish, unhappiness”).
Suffix Used to form an adjective meaning "possession of or relation to" from nouns ending in -oma or -omata . By surface analysis, -omat(a) +‎ -ous .
Suffix ( rare ) Synonym of -opia (“seeing”). From Ancient Greek ὄψις (ópsis, “aspect, appearance”).

Suffix (informal, usually derogatory) Used with adjectives ending in -y to form nicknames based on a negative quality of a person. Usage Note Usually the adjective must be two syllables long and end in -y , potentially with an interfix if the original adjective ends in a different sound. As with fancypants , usage has not yet settled as to whether this should be separate, linked with a hyphen as a suffixoid, or fused like a normal affix. Extracted from fancypants .
Suffix Used to form the names of disorders and phenomena relating to words and speech. From Ancient Greek φάσις (phásis, “utterance”), from φημί (phēmí, “I say”).
/pɹəf.ən/, /ˈpɹoʊ.fən/, /ˈpɹəʊ.fən/ Suffix ( pharmacology ) Used to form names of ibuprofen derivatives used as anti-inflammatory agents. From ibuprofen .
Suffix Having wings ( of a specified size, type or number ) From Ancient Greek πτερ(όν) (pter(ón), “wing”) +‎ -ous .

Suffix Denotes an aesthetically-oriented genre of speculative fiction based on the noun to which it is suffixed, usually involving ahistorical or anachronistic technology and its effects on society. First used when coining cyberpunk or as a back-formation to coin steampunk . Probably from the influence of the punk subculture on these genres.
/kwiːn/, /kwɪn/ Suffix ( pharmacology ) Used to form names of quinoline derivatives. Contraction of quinoline .
Suffix (anime and manga, fandom slang) Appended to a person's name or nickname to convey honour and respect. Borrowed from Japanese さま (-sama).
/stə.ɹaɪd/ Suffix ( pharmacology ) Used to form names of testosterone reductase inhibitors.

Suffix Forms the names of types of electronic devices and systems. Also used to form the name of a number of electronics and technology companies. Formed from a rebracketing of electronics as elec + -tronics , rather than the original electron + -ic + -s ; first attested in molectronics (1959)/ moletronics (1962). Equivalent to -tron +‎ -ic +‎ -s .
Suffix ( zoology ) Used to categorise animals based on their evolutionary origin, life history, growth-form or ecological preferences.
Noun ( firearms ) A standard kind of firearm designed to fire bullets that are approximately 0.45 inch in diameter.

Proper Noun (computing, Microsoft) A set of Microsoft products and services – primarily the.NET Framework, which permits the development of software for a virtual machine in any programming language that is CLI-compliant (i.e., conforms with the Common Language Infrastructure). Usually said to be from network . Called in early press announcements Next Generation Windows Services before this name was chosen. According to Justin Grant, who was part of the team on the Microsoft campus, the name...

Symbol (Internet slang, tone indicator) Denotes that the preceding statement has a neutral connotation. From / + abbreviation of neutral , using the tone indicator format of slash-prefixing set by the earlier /s (“sarcasm”).
Proper Noun A book of the Catholic and Eastern Orthodox canon of the Old Testament, considered apocryphal by Protestants. Synonym: ( abbreviation ) 1 Macc.
Noun Something that is perfect. Adjective Ideal; impossible to improve. From the highest rating on the 1-10 scale.
Proper Noun ( law ) Abbreviation of United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit .
Noun The decade from 1720 to 1729.
Noun The decade from 1830 to 1839.
Noun The decade from 1940 to 1949.

Noun A tool used in machining fields, especially milling, to aid in setup. It is a block of steel that is precisely squared and parallel whose sides are 2, 4, and 6 inches long, respectively. 2-4-6 blocks are a larger version of the more common 1-2-3 block.
Noun Under the Whyte notation system, a Mallet-type locomotive with two leading wheels on a leading truck, two sets of eight driving wheels, and four trailing wheels on a trailing truck.
Noun (organic chemistry, IUPAC name) isoprene

Phrase Used playfully or sarcastically to mock unhelpful creative feedback, critiquing without giving any specifics. Used to describe something that needs to be cooler, suggesting that it lacks the sufficient coolness. From the 2011 episode Suited for Success , the fourteenth episode of the first season of the animated series My Little Pony: Friendship Is Magic , in which Rainbow Dash says “It needs to be about 20% cooler,” vaguely critiquing one of Rarity's dress designs.
Adjective Abbreviation of twenty-twenty .
Proper Noun ( US politics ) Abbreviation of Second Amendment .
Proper Noun ( biblical ) A book of the Old Testament of Bible, and of the Tanakh. Synonyms: 1 Kings, ( abbreviation ) 3 Kgs

Noun ( baseball ) Third base, third baseman ( baseball ) triple, a baseball statistic indicating a runner has safely advanced to third base ( British English ) A grade of pencil with lead that makes darker marks than a pencil grade 2B but lighter marks than a pencil of grade 4B. ( oncology ) A subcategory of stage 3 cancer.
Noun A device that analyzes a real-world object or environment to collect data on its shape and possibly its color.
Noun Initialism of third-party logistics .
Noun Under the Whyte notation system, a Mallet-type locomotive with four leading wheels on a leading truck, two sets of eight driving wheels, and two trailing wheels on a trailing truck.

Proper Noun In the United States, a youth organization administered by the Cooperative Extension System of the United States Department of Agriculture with the mission of "engaging youth to reach their fullest potential while advancing the field of youth development." Derived from the four beginning letters of "Head, Heart, Hands, and Health", the organization's former motto.

/fɔːtiː keɪ/, /ˈfɔɹti keɪ/ Proper Noun (informal, slang, science fiction) Warhammer 40,000 , a British tabletop military game set in a dystopian future Galaxy torn by war. Usage Note Warhammer 40,000 The number 40,000 in general A 40-kilometer race 40 K: potassium-40 From 40 +‎ k . From 40,000, part of "Warhammer 40,000", referring to the future year where the game was set in.
Noun ( paper ) Abbreviation of quarto , a paper size. ( printing ) Abbreviation of quarto , a corresponding book size. From Latin quārtō , ablative case singular of quārtus (“fourth”).
Noun US standard spelling of 5000 metres .
Adjective Abbreviation of fiftieth .

Noun ( humorous ) An extremely complicated strategy involving deception and ulterior motives, especially in politics. Synonym: 12D chess ( humorous ) Short for five-dimensional chess , suggesting an even more complicated variant of 3D chess or 4D chess.

Noun ( biochemistry ) A specially altered nucleotide end to the 5′ end of precursor messenger RNA and some other primary RNA transcripts as found in eukaryotes and caliciviruses, vital to creating mature messenger RNA which is then able to undergo translation.
Noun ( geometry ) Synonym of hexagon : A polygon with six sides and six angles. From 6 +‎ -gon .
Adjective Abbreviation of sixty-third .

Noun ( bowling ) A split where the farthest-left and farthest-right pins are the only pins left standing. If the pins are numbered left to right from the bottom, the remaining two pins are numbers 7 and 10.
Adjective Abbreviation of ninety-second .
Adjective Abbreviation of ninety-fourth .
/ˌækəˈpɛlə/, /ˌɑːkəˈpɛlə/ Adverb Misspelling of a cappella . Adjective Misspelling of a cappella .
Adverb Obsolete form of o'clock .
Phrase ( somewhat dated ) Synonym of six of one, half a dozen of the other

/ˌæləˈməʊd/, /ˌɑləˈməʊd/ Adjective Fashionable; in the current style or fashion. Synonym: fashionable ( US ) Served with ice cream. ( cooking ) Of beef: larded and stewed with vegetables. Adverb In a particular style or fashion. Unadapted borrowing from French à la mode (“in fashion”). The US sense was coined by polyglot restaurant owner John Gieriet in Minnesota in the 1800s though later attributed to Berry Hall and Charles Watson Townsend.
Adjective ( set phrase ) In-process, delayed, awaited, or deserved for a considerable duration of time; overdue.

word: a magician never reveals his secrets
definition: Phrase A polite refusal by someone who has just done a magic trick to reveal how it works. ( by extension ) A refusal to explain how one accomplished something impressive.

Phrase Several. Several of. Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see hang,‎ on. Usage Note This is a leading example of the structure of a partitive construction. Other words that behave the same way as number does are dozen , quantity , score , hundred , army , lakh , mob , lot , plethora , myriad , herd .

Noun ( military ) The innermost circle of a nuclear explosion, within which all structures are destroyed. The letter A designates the first (measured from ground zero); successive outer rings were designated B , C , etc.

word: a sheet in the wind's eye
definition: Adjective Drunk. See three sheets to the wind .

Noun (US, military) A military ration consisting of fresh, refrigerated, or frozen foods.
Adjective Shaped like the capital letter " A ".
Noun Initialism of autograph letter .
Noun ( music ) A 440 Hertz musical pitch, which serves as the tuning standard for the note A above middle C in concert pitch.
Proper Noun Initialism of Association for the Advancement of Agricultural Sciences in Africa . Initialism of Australian and Allied All Services Association .
Noun ( military ) Initialism of amphibious assault bulk fuel system .
/ˌæb.oʊˈmaɪ.sɪn/, /ˌæb.əʊˈmaɪ.sɪn/ Noun venturicidin From Latin aabomyceticus +‎ -in , after the bacterium Streptomyces hygroscopicus subsp. aabomyceticus .

/ˌæ.bəˈkɑt.i/ Noun Synonym of avocado . Borrowed from Portuguese abacate . Doublet of avocado .
/ˈæ.bə.kəˌʃi/, /ˌæ.bə.kəˈʃi/ Noun A large Brazilian pineapple. Borrowed from Brazilian Portuguese abacaxi (“pineapple”).
Preposition (British English, US, dialectal) Behind; on the other side of From aback +‎ of .

/ˌæbˌeɪ.li.əˈneɪ.ʃən/, /ˌæbˌeɪl.jəˈneɪ.ʃən/ Noun ( law ) The act of abalienating; alienation; estrangement; transferring a legal title. The transfer of property, such as land, goods, or chattels, from one to another. From Latin abalienatio . Equivalent to abalienate +‎ -ion .
Adjective Able to be abandoned; suitable for abandonment. From abandon +‎ -able .
/əˈbæʃəbəl/ Adjective which can be abashed From abash +‎ -able .
Proper Noun A surname.

/əˈbeɪt.mənt/ Noun The act of abating, or the state of being abated; a lessening, diminution, or reduction; a moderation; removal or putting an end to; the suppression. ( law ) The action of a person that abates, or without proper authority enters a residence after the death of the owner and before the heir takes possession. ( law ) The...
Adjective ( rare ) Resembling or characteristic of an abattoir. From abattoir +‎ -like .
Noun ( numismatics ) The monetary unit of Georgia until 1833, divided 40 puli. Borrowed from Georgian აბაზი (abazi). Doublet of abbasi .
Noun A genetic disorder characterized by albinism, a black lock of hair, cell migration disorder of the neurocytes of the gut, and sensorineural deafness. From initial letters of the traits.
/ˈæb.dæbz/ Noun ( slang ) Extreme nervousness or anxiety; terror; heebie-jeebies. Unknown. Possibly imitative of the spluttering speech of one who is extremely nervous or anxious.
Noun The presence of the viscera outside of the body, typically through a wound
Adjective ( anatomy ) abdominal and cranial From abdomino- +‎ cranial .

/æbˌdɑm.ɪ.noʊ.di.ə.fɹæɡˈmæt.ɪk bɹiːðɪŋ/ Noun ( medicine ) A type of breathing used to treat dyspnea, where the patient used the abdominal muscles for the expiration and the diaphragm for the inspiration.
Proper Noun A surname.
Noun A type of anticoagulant medication.
/ˌeɪbəˈ-/, /ˌæbəˈloʊ.ni.ən/, /ˌæbəˈləʊ.ni.ən/ Noun (Christianity, historical) Synonym of Abelian .
/abəˈlʊŋɡuː/ Noun (South Africa, now chiefly derogatory) White people collectively.
Proper Noun A locality in the Bathurst council area, central eastern New South Wales, Australia.

/ˌæb.ɚˈdinˌʃaɪ.ɚ/, /ˌæb.ɚˈdinˌʃɚ/ Proper Noun A council area in north-east Scotland, created in 1996 on the abolition of Grampian Region. (The city of Aberdeen is separate and has its own council.) A historical county of Scotland which was absorbed into Grampian Region in 1975. From Aberdeen +‎ -shire .

Proper Noun A surname. From Sanskrit. This etymology is incomplete. You can help Wiktionary by elaborating on the origins of this term.
Proper Noun A female given name from Hebrew. From Hebrew אביה , name of minor biblical characters.
/ˌeɪ.baɪ.əˈlɑd͡ʒ.ə.kli/, /ˌeɪ.baɪ.əˈlɑd͡ʒ.ɪ.kə.li/ Adverb ( biology ) In an abiological manner. [Late 19 th century.] From abiological +‎ -ly or abiologic +‎ -ally or a- +‎ biologically .
Proper Noun A village in Kiruna municipality, Norrbotten County, Lapland, Sweden.
Verb ( transitive ) To treat or regard as abject. From abject +‎ -ify .

[First attested around 1350 to 1470.] A repudiation on oath of a religious or political principle. [Mid 17 th century.] The act of abjuring. First attested around 1439. From Middle English abjuracioun , from Latin abiūrātiō (“forswearing, abjuration”), from ab (“from, away from”) + iūrō (“swear or take an oath”), from iūs (“law, right, duty”). Compare French ...

Kingdom of Abkhazia (a former kingdom in the Caucasus region). Borrowed from Russian Абха́з...
Adjective Exhibiting, characteristic of, or related to ablenormativity. From able +‎ normative .

Verb (neologism, artificial intelligence, computing) To uncensor a large language model by modifying specific model internals to remove refusal behaviours or unwanted traits, while aiming to preserve the model's other capabilities. Blend of ablate +‎ obliterate . Coined by Redditor /u/FailSpai in early 2024, as the idea is to ablate refusal features to the point of obliteration .
Proper Noun A barangay of Mauban, Quezon, Philippines.

/əˈbɔɹtɪd/ Adjective Stopped before completion; especially because of problems or danger. Brought forth prematurely. Checked in normal development at an early stage. /əˌbaʊt ˈʃɪp/ Verb ( intransitive ) Tack; to cause to turn into the wind and through the other side ending with a full 180 degree turn. Usage Note Usually used as an order or command. From the imperative phrase used as an order aboard sailing ships.

Noun ( titular ) Abbreviation of archbishop .

Noun (archaic, UK slang) A British banknote. [18th c.] From Abraham Newland (1730–1807), chief cashier at the Bank of England, whose signature appeared on every banknote issued by the Bank from 1782 to 1807.

/æˈbɹin/, /ˈeɪ.bɹin/ Noun An toxic amino acid obtained from jequirity beans; C 12 H 14 N 2 O 2 , that is different than abrin. From abrin .
Adverb ( medicine ) Abbreviation of absente febre ; in the absence of fever.
Adjective That leads to the production of abscesses From abscess +‎ -genic .
/æbˈsiːkɒn/ Proper Noun A city in Atlantic County, New Jersey, United States.

Noun ( set theory ) The set that contains exactly those elements belonging to the universal set but not to a given set. Usage Note In mathematical expressions, the absolute complement of a given set A is denoted by "A c ."

Noun Obsolete spelling of absolviture . Misspelling of absolvitor . See absolviture and absolvitor , as applicable.
